From Friday, October 23, Foundry work runs in two-week sprints. Every student runs every sprint,
whether you are staffed on a client engagement, on a studio project, or between the two. Each
sprint you say what you will do, do it, show it working, and say what happened.

The sprint replaces the weekly update email. Your sprint plan, review, and Loom demo are how
Professor Murff, your teammates, and the Foundry know what you are working on.

## The fall sprints

| Sprint | Starts | Plan due | Wrap-up and certification due | Certification deliverable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fri, Oct 23 | Mon, Oct 26, 11:59 PM | Fri, Nov 6, 8:00 AM | A Skill or custom command, plus hooks (Claude Code in Action) |
| 2 | Fri, Nov 6 | Mon, Nov 9, 11:59 PM | Fri, Nov 20, 8:00 AM | An MCP server (Introduction to MCP) |
| 3 | Fri, Nov 20 | Mon, Nov 23, 11:59 PM | Fri, Dec 4, 8:00 AM | A written answer to your weakest exam domain, with code (Prep Course) |

A sprint starts and ends at the Friday studio. The Wrap-up is due at 8:00 AM, when studio
starts, so studio that day can open with demos.

Each sprint is worth 100 points across two Canvas assignments, **Sprint N Plan** (10) and
**Sprint N Wrap-up** (90). The certification deliverable is a third assignment, worth 20, due at
the same time as the Wrap-up. See [Grading](01-syllabus.qmd#grading) in the syllabus for how
these add up.

## Staffed or not, you sprint

Engagement length is set with each client, and engagements start and end on the client's
schedule. The sprint calendar does not move with them. Whatever you are working on during a
sprint is what you plan, build, and demo.

| If during the sprint you are | You sprint on |
|---|---|
| On a client engagement | Your part of the engagement |
| On a [studio project](09-studio-projects.qmd) | The studio project |
| Between engagements | A studio project, or internal Foundry work Professor Murff or a Foundry leader assigns you |

Every plan names at least one person, other than you and Professor Murff, who will use or see
the work: the client, a user, or a teammate who depends on it. Work with no one at the other end
is an exercise, and `/sprint-plan` will ask you who that person is.

**When your staffing changes mid-sprint,** run `/sprint-plan` again. It records what changed and
why, and your work is read against the plan as it stands at the end. Being staffed, unstaffed,
or moved partway through a sprint costs nothing.

**On a team,** everyone plans, reviews, and demos on their own. Teammates often share a goal.
Your plan says which part of it is yours, and your Output is graded on that part, with the
team's result as context.

## What you turn in

| Deliverable | What it is | Where it lives | How you turn it in | When | Points |
|---|---|---|---|---|--:|
| **Plan** | What you will do, for whom, your part of it, why, how you will know it is done, and how hard you expect it to be. `/sprint-plan` writes it with you | `sprints/sprint-N-plan.md` in your Foundry repo | Commit it, and paste its GitHub link into **Sprint N Plan** on Canvas | The Monday after the sprint starts, 11:59 PM | 10 |
| **Output** | What you finished this sprint: code, a deployed change, an agent or automation, research, a design, a client deliverable | The client repo, your studio repo, a link, or your demo | Nothing separate. List every place it lives under **Where the work lives** in your README | Wrap-up due date | 50 |
| **Review** | What `/sprint-review` produces: a report on your sprint, then your answers to its retro questions | `sprints/sprint-N-review.md` in your Foundry repo | Commit it, and paste its GitHub link into **Sprint N Wrap-up** on Canvas | Wrap-up due date | 20 |
| **Demo** | 2 to 3 minutes on Loom of your work, working | Loom | Paste the Loom link into **Sprint N Wrap-up** on Canvas | Wrap-up due date | 20 |

### Your Foundry repo

Your plans and reviews live in your own repo, made from the
[builder template](https://github.com/byu-strategy/builder-template), the same template MSB 341
uses. Name it `<your NetID>_foundry`, keep it private, and add Professor Murff (`sdmurff`) as a
collaborator. If you also take MSB 341, keep the two repos separate: each course numbers its
sprints differently.

Your client code does not go in this repo. It stays in the engagement's repo in the
`ai-foundry-byu` organization, which Professor Murff can already see. Your Foundry repo holds
your plans, your reviews, and a README that says where the work lives.

The first time you run `/sprint-plan` in the repo, it asks which course the repo is for. Answer
AI Foundry. We set this up together in studio on October 23.

### The plan

Run `/sprint-plan` on the first day of the sprint. It interviews you and writes
`sprints/sprint-N-plan.md`:

```markdown
# Sprint N Plan

**Engagement:** The client, your studio project, or the internal work.

**Teammates:** Who else is working on it, or "Solo."

**Goal:** What will be true in two weeks that is not true now?

**My part:** Which part of the goal is yours.

**Who will see it:** The client, user, or teammate who will use or see the work,
and what they will see.

**Why this:** Why is this the right next thing?

**Done looks like:** How will you know the goal was met? Specific enough that
someone else could check.

**Certification:** What you will build for this sprint's certification
deliverable, and where it will live.

**Predicted difficulty:** 1 to 5.
```

On time, with every field filled in, earns all 10 points. The plan is graded for completion, and
your predicted difficulty is not graded. Aim high.

**You can change the plan.** Plans change once you learn something, and on client work they
change when the client does. Run `/sprint-plan` again during the sprint. It asks what is changing
and why, updates the plan, adds a dated note, and commits it. There is nothing to resubmit on
Canvas: your plan link always shows the current file. A change with no note is the one thing to
avoid, because nobody reading the plan can then tell what you set out to do.

### The review

On or before the Wrap-up due date, run `/sprint-review` in your Foundry repo. It shows you the
projects you worked in during the sprint and asks which ones belong to this sprint, including the
client repo. It reads only the projects you confirm, then writes a report: when you worked, where
you got stuck and how you got unstuck, what took the most time, and which Builder axes your work
advanced. Nothing leaves your computer except the report.

Then it asks six retro questions:

1. Did you hit the goal? Yes, partly, or no, and why.
2. What did the client or your users say or do about the work?
3. What did the report show you that you did not expect?
4. If the plan changed, why?
5. Actual difficulty, 1 to 5, and why it differed from what you predicted.
6. What will you change next sprint?

Answer in your own words. It saves your answers exactly as you write them at the bottom of
`sprints/sprint-N-review.md`, then commits and pushes the file.

### The demo

Record 2 to 3 minutes on [Loom](https://www.loom.com) of your work, working, with real content.
No intro and no reflection: the work itself, opened, for most of the video. On a team, show your
part and say what you did.

| If your sprint was | Your demo shows |
|---|---|
| A feature or a deployed change | The feature in use: click through it |
| An agent, automation, or integration | It running, start to finish, on a real input |
| An evaluation harness or tests | The tests running and the results they return |
| Discovery or research | One or two of your notes opened, and what you concluded |
| A client deliverable (memo, deck, plan) | The deliverable, and the decision it asks the client to make |
| Design | The interface or designs, clicked or scrolled through |

**Loom only.** A demo on Google Drive, YouTube, or an uploaded file scores 0. Set the Loom to
"Anyone with the link" or share it with scott.murff@byu.edu. A video Professor Murff cannot open
is not graded until it is shared.

**Client confidentiality.** Loom is an outside service. If your engagement's confidentiality
terms do not allow recording the client's data, demo the same work on sample or fake data, and
say so at the start of the video. If you are not sure what your client allows, ask Professor
Murff before you record.

Keep real names, emails, and phone numbers off the screen.

### The Wrap-up

Submit two links in **Sprint N Wrap-up** on Canvas: your review file on GitHub and your Loom.
Before you do, make sure the **Where the work lives** section of your README lists every repo,
deployed app, and document someone needs to check your output.

## Grading rubric

| Category | Points | What earns full marks |
|---|--:|---|
| **Plan** | 10 | Its GitHub link submitted on Canvas by the Monday deadline, with every field filled in. Graded for completion |
| **Output** | 50 | Your part of the goal, real, finished, and checkable. Read against your plan as it stands at the end, and, from Sprint 2 on, weighed by how hard the work was for you. A goal that needs someone else's yes is graded on the asks you made |
| **Review** | 20 | Report committed, with your retro answering all six questions and responding to something specific in the report |
| **Demo** | 20 | 2 to 3 minutes on Loom of your work, working, with real or clearly labeled sample content, viewable by Professor Murff |

**Output on client work.** A client engagement does not always produce something new every two
weeks: a client goes quiet, a data export is late, a decision waits on their meeting. Output is
read against what was in your control. Record what you were waiting on, when you asked, and what
you did meanwhile, and that work is graded as output.

**Goals that need someone else to say yes.** A client sign-off, a user agreeing to test, a
meeting booked: you control the asks, not the answers. For these goals, Output is graded on the
asks you made and can show: who you asked, when, what you asked for, and what they said. A no or
a "not yet" costs no points when the ask is on record and your retro says what you learned.

**Demo length.** A demo up to 3:30 loses no points. From Sprint 2, each started 30 seconds past
3:30 costs 1 point (3:31 to 4:00 is minus 1, 4:01 to 4:30 minus 2, and so on).

**Late work.** Canvas applies the late penalty: 10% per day, up to 9 days. Graders never deduct
for lateness themselves.

## The certification deliverable

Each fall sprint carries one course from the [certification track](08-certification.qmd) and the
thing that course has you build. It is its own Canvas assignment, **Certification:
&lt;course&gt;**, worth 20 points and due with the Wrap-up.

| Part | Points | What earns full marks |
|---|--:|---|
| **Certificate** | 5 | The course's certificate of completion from the Anthropic Academy, as a PDF or screenshot |
| **Working deliverable** | 15 | The deliverable in a repo, used in your real work (client engagement or studio project), and shown working in your sprint demo or a separate Loom of up to 2 minutes |

Build the deliverable into the sprint's work where you can. A Skill your team uses on the client
repo counts as both sprint output and the certification deliverable.

If you finished Building with the Claude API and built its evaluation harness this fall, you may
submit the harness in place of any one of the three deliverables. Say so in that sprint's plan.

## Your sprint feedback

After each sprint is graded, your score appears in Canvas, and your sprint report appears on the
**Builder** tab of your profile in the Foundry app, [aifoundry.byu.edu/app](https://aifoundry.byu.edu/app).
The report shows how each category was scored, what your work showed on the Builder axes, and
what to do next sprint.

**Questions about your sprint feedback:** reply to the Canvas comment your score came with,
saying which part of the report you mean and what you think was missed. Professor Murff reads
every reply.
